lessons.title: Overview of the Onion Industry
lessons.body: Onion farming is one of the most profitable agricultural ventures in Africa, with steady demand across local and export markets. In 2022, Africa produced over 20 million tonnes of onions, with Egypt, Nigeria, and South Africa leading. Onions are a staple in every African kitchen, used in soups, stews, and salads. The industry includes smallholder farmers, commercial growers, and traders. For a beginner, onions offer a quick return: you can harvest within 90-120 days from transplanting. The main challenge is post-harvest losses, which can reach 30-50% due to poor storage. But with proper techniques, you can reduce losses and increase profit. Start small: a 0.5-hectare plot can yield 10-15 tonnes if managed well. Key success factors are quality seed, proper spacing, and timely pest control. In Kenya, for example, a farmer can earn KES 500,000 per hectare per season if selling at KES 50 per kg. The market is always thereâonions are never out of season in demand. You can sell to local markets, hotels, or processers. The industry is growing due to urbanization and population growth. However, competition is high, so focus on quality and consistency. Learn from experienced farmers, join cooperatives, and keep records. This module will give you the foundation to start your onion farming journey with confidence.

lessons.title: Types of Onions: Bulb, Bunching, and Shallots
lessons.body: There are three main types of onions you can grow in Africa: bulb onions, bunching onions (also called spring onions or scallions), and shallots. Bulb onions are the most common, forming a large, round bulb. They are used in cooking and can be stored for months. Popular varieties include Red Creole, Texas Grano, and Bombay Red. Bunching onions are harvested young for their green leaves and mild flavor. They are ready in 60-80 days and sell well in urban markets. Shallots are small, mild-flavored bulbs that grow in clusters. They are prized in West African cuisine, especially in Ghana and Nigeria. Each type has different management. Bulb onions need well-drained soil, full sun, and 4-6 months to mature. Bunching onions can be grown densely and harvested earlier. Shallots are planted from small bulbs and multiply. For beginners, start with bulb onions because of high demand and storage life. But if you have a market for fresh greens, bunching onions give quick cash. Shallots fetch premium prices but have a smaller market. Choose based on your local demand and climate. In dry areas, bulb onions do well with irrigation. In humid areas, bunching onions are less prone to rot. Always buy certified seed or sets from reputable suppliers. Avoid using onions from the market as seedâthey may carry diseases. Test a small plot before scaling up.

lessons.title: Global Production and Market Trends
lessons.body: Global onion production reached about 100 million tonnes in 2022, with China, India, and the United States as top producers. In Africa, Egypt leads with 3.5 million tonnes, followed by Nigeria (1.5 million tonnes) and South Africa (0.7 million tonnes). The demand for onions is rising due to population growth and changing diets. In West Africa, countries like Senegal and Ivory Coast import onions, creating opportunities for local farmers. Prices fluctuate seasonally: during the dry season, prices can double because supply is low. For example, in Ghana, a 50kg bag of onions can sell for GHS 300 during scarcity but GHS 150 during harvest. To succeed, you must understand market trends. Key trends include: increased demand for red onions in urban areas, growth in processed onion products (powder, paste), and export opportunities to Europe and the Middle East. However, exports require strict quality standards, such as uniform size and no blemishes. For local markets, focus on freshness and competitive pricing. Use market information from sources like Esoko or local agricultural extension officers. Plan your planting to harvest when prices are highâusually 3-4 months after the main harvest. Store onions properly to sell later. Join a cooperative to access better markets and negotiate prices. With good planning, onion farming can be a reliable income source.

lessons.title: Nutritional and Economic Importance
lessons.body: Onions are packed with nutrients that are essential for health. A 100g serving provides about 40 calories, 1.1g protein, 9.3g carbohydrates, and 1.7g fiber. They are rich in vitamin C, vitamin B6, potassium, and antioxidants like quercetin. These compounds help reduce inflammation, lower cholesterol, and boost immunity. In many African cultures, onions are also used traditionally to treat colds and infections. Economically, onions are a cash crop that can transform livelihoods. A smallholder farmer with 1 hectare can earn between $2,000 and $5,000 per season, depending on market prices. In Nigeria, onion farming employs over 1 million people, from production to trading. The value chain includes seed suppliers, farmers, transporters, wholesalers, and retailers. Women are heavily involved in onion trading, especially in West Africa. Onions also contribute to food security because they are used daily in cooking. Unlike other crops, onions have a long shelf life if stored properly, allowing farmers to sell when prices are favorable. They can be processed into powder, paste, or pickles, adding value. For example, a kilogram of onion powder can sell for $10, compared to $1 for fresh onions. This creates opportunities for small-scale processing. By growing onions, you not only feed your family but also create jobs and income for your community.

lessons.title: Basic Botany of the Onion Plant
lessons.body: Understanding the botany of the onion plant helps you grow it better. Onions (Allium cepa) are biennial plants, meaning they complete their life cycle in two years. In the first year, they grow leaves and form a bulb. In the second year, they flower and produce seeds. The plant has a shallow root system, mostly in the top 30cm of soil, so it needs frequent, light irrigation. The leaves are tubular and hollow, and they manufacture food through photosynthesis. The bulb is actually a modified underground stem made of fleshy scales. When days get longer (more than 12 hours of daylight), the plant starts forming bulbs. This is why day length matters: varieties are classified as short-day, intermediate, or long-day. In Africa, short-day varieties like Red Creole are best for equatorial regions. The flower stalk emerges from the center of the bulb, bearing a cluster of small white flowers. Seeds are small, black, and angular. Onions also have a pungent smell due to sulfur compounds. These compounds are released when cells are damaged, making you cry. Pests like thrips and diseases like purple blotch attack the leaves. Proper spacing (10-15cm between plants) ensures good air circulation. Crop rotation with cereals or legumes helps prevent soil-borne diseases. Knowing these basics will guide your management decisions.

lessons.title: Career Opportunities in Onion Farming
lessons.body: Onion farming offers many career paths beyond just growing. You can become a seed producer, a nursery specialist, or a pest management expert. Seed production is lucrative: a kilogram of certified onion seed can sell for $50-$100. To produce seed, you need to grow onions for two years and manage flowering. Nursery operators raise seedlings for farmers who prefer transplants. They can earn $0.02 per seedling, and with 100,000 seedlings, that's $2,000 per cycle. As a farm manager, you can oversee large onion farms for absentee owners, earning a monthly salary. Agricultural extension officers advise farmers on best practices. Trading and brokerage: buy onions from farmers and sell to urban markets or processors. A trader can make a 20-30% margin. Processing: turn onions into powder, paste, or pickles. This requires a grinder, dryer, and packaging machine. Storage: build ventilated stores and charge farmers for storage. Transport: own a truck and move onions from farms to markets. Agribusiness consultants help farmers with business plans and market linkages. If you love teaching, become a trainer or write guides. Many NGOs and government programs hire onion experts. You can also start a cooperative to aggregate produce and negotiate better prices. With skills in record-keeping and marketing, you can scale any of these. The key is to start small, learn, and reinvest. Onion farming is not just a jobâit's a business ecosystem with room for everyone.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Onion Farming Essentials for African Agribusiness

This practical reference distils the operational knowledge you need to move from understanding onions to producing and selling them profitably. It is written for African agribusiness operators â smallholder commercial farmers, aggregators, and agripreneurs â who treat onion farming as a business, not a subsistence activity. Onions (Allium cepa) are among the most traded horticultural crops in Africa, and the difference between profit and loss usually comes down to variety choice, water discipline, storage, and market timing.

1. The Onion Plant: What You Must Know to Manage It

The onion is a biennial plant grown as an annual. In year one it produces a bulb; in year two it bolts to flower and seed. Understanding this lifecycle is critical because any stress that convinces the plant it has "completed" its first year â drought, extreme cold, or nitrogen shortage early on â will trigger bolting and destroy bulb quality.

  • Root system: shallow and fibrous, mostly in the top 15â20 cm of soil. This is why onions cannot compete with weeds and why drip irrigation and frequent light watering outperform deep flooding.
  • Leaves (tops): tubular, waxy, and the engine of bulb growth. Each leaf corresponds to a bulb scale. More healthy leaves = bigger bulb.
  • Bulb: formed when day length and temperature trigger the plant to stop leaf growth and transfer sugars into storage scales. This is why day-length type determines which variety you can grow at your latitude.
  • Day-length classes: short-day (<10â12 hrs) for latitudes below ~28Â°; intermediate (12â14 hrs); long-day (>14 hrs) for temperate zones. Most of sub-Saharan Africa sits in the short-day and intermediate zones.

2. Variety Selection: The Single Biggest Profit Lever

Planting the wrong day-length type is the most common and most expensive mistake in African onion farming. A long-day variety grown in Kenya, Nigeria, or Ghana will produce leaves but no bulb. Conversely, a short-day variety grown in the Mediterranean will bolt prematurely. Match variety to latitude, then to market preference (red vs. white vs. yellow), then to storage life.

Table 1: Onion Types and Their Commercial Characteristics
Type Botanical / Common Name Typical Use Storage Life Key African Markets
Bulb onion (red) Allium cepa â Red Creole, Bombay Red Fresh market, salads, cooking 2â4 months Kenya, Tanzania, Nigeria, Ghana
Bulb onion (white/yellow) Allium cepa â Texas Grano, Superex Processing, dehydration, long storage 5â8 months South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia
Bunching onion Allium fistulosum â Welsh onion, spring onion Fresh greens, high-value urban markets 1â2 weeks (fresh) Nairobi, Lagos, Accra urban chains
Shallot Allium cepa var. aggregatum Premium culinary, export to Europe 4â6 months Madagascar, Ghana, Burkina Faso

Sources: FAO, Onion: Post-harvest Operations (2023); International Trade Centre, Onion Market Brief (2022); Brewster, J.L., CABI (2008).

3. Global and African Production and Market Trends

Global onion production exceeds 100 million tonnes annually, dominated by China and India. Africa contributes roughly 10â12% of world output, led by Egypt, Nigeria, Sudan, and South Africa. The commercial opportunity for African producers is not in competing with China on volume but in capturing (a) import substitution in markets where onions are imported at high cost, (b) regional cross-border trade, and (c) off-season windows when northern hemisphere supply is short.

Table 2: Leading African Onion Producers and Market Context
Country Approx. Annual Production Main Production Zones Business Significance
Egypt 3.0â3.5 million t Nile Delta, Upper Egypt Major exporter to Europe, Gulf, and sub-Saharan Africa
Nigeria 1.5â2.0 million t Sokoto, Kano, Kaduna Large domestic demand; seasonal price volatility
Sudan 0.7â1.0 million t Gezira, River Nile State Export to Gulf and East Africa
South Africa 0.6â0.8 million t Western Cape, Free State Industrial-scale, export-oriented
Kenya 0.2â0.3 million t Kajiado, Narok, Meru Imports from Tanzania and Ethiopia; urban demand strong

Sources: FAO FAOSTAT (2023); African Development Bank, Horticulture Value Chains in Africa (2021); ITC Trade Map (2023).

4. Nutritional and Economic Importance

Onions are a low-cost source of dietary fibre, vitamin C, vitamin B6, folate, potassium, and bioactive sulphur compounds (allicin, quercetin) associated with cardiovascular and anti-inflammatory benefits. Economically, onions are a "cash-flow crop": they store for months, can be sold in small units, and are demanded daily by households and food services. For African agribusinesses, the value chain includes seed/seedling supply, irrigation services, aggregation, curing, storage, and transport â each a business opportunity.

5. Practical Operations: The Critical Control Points

  1. Soil and pH: well-drained loam or sandy loam, pH 6.0â6.8. Test before planting. Onions are intolerant of waterlogging and salinity.
  2. Nursery: 4â6 weeks, raised beds or trays, light shade, daily light watering. Transplant at 10â15 cm height, pencil-thickness.
  3. Spacing: 10â15 cm between plants, 25â30 cm between rows for bulb onions; tighter for bunching types.
  4. Fertility: phosphorus at planting, split nitrogen during leaf growth, stop nitrogen 4â6 weeks before harvest to improve curing and storage.
  5. Irrigation: drip or furrow; keep top 20 cm moist but never saturated. Stop irrigation 2â3 weeks before harvest.
  6. Pest and disease: thrips, onion fly, downy mildew, purple blotch, and neck rot. Rotate with cereals, avoid overhead irrigation late in the season, and use certified seed.
  7. Harvest: when 50â70% of tops fall and necks soften. Lift on a dry day, cure in the field or under shade for 2â3 weeks until necks are dry and skins rustle.
  8. Storage: cool, dry, ventilated, dark. Well-cured yellow onions store 5â8 months; red onions 2â4 months. Poor curing is the leading cause of post-harvest loss (30â50% in parts of Africa).

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pesticide Handling

Onion crops are frequently treated with insecticides (e.g., for thrips) and fungicides. Always read the label and observe the pre-harvest interval (PHI) â the minimum days between the last spray and harvest. In many African markets, residue violations cause consignments to be rejected at export and create health risks locally. Wear gloves, boots, a mask, and long clothing when spraying; never spray against the wind; never eat, drink, or smoke during application; store chemicals locked away from children, food, and animal feed; and triple-rinse empty containers before safe disposal. Where possible, use integrated pest management (IPM) â certified seed, rotation, sticky traps, and biological controls â to reduce chemical reliance.

6. Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Confirm your latitude and choose a short-day or intermediate variety accordingly â never plant a long-day variety in the tropics.
  • â Soil tested: pH 6.0â6.8, well-drained, organic matter incorporated before planting.
  • â Certified seed or healthy transplants from a reputable nursery; no signs of damping-off or thrips.
  • â Irrigation plan in place â drip preferred; water stress avoided during bulb swelling.
  • â Nitrogen stopped 4â6 weeks before expected harvest; irrigation stopped 2â3 weeks before.
  • â Harvest at 50â70% top fall; cure 2â3 weeks until necks are dry and skins rustle.
  • â Storage: cool, dark, ventilated; graded and sorted to remove damaged bulbs before storage.
  • â Market plan: identify buyer, price window, and transport before harvest â not after.

7. Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO FAOSTAT â Crop and Livestock Production Data (free global and country-level onion production statistics).
  • FAO â Onion Post-Harvest Operations (INPhO) (free technical guide on curing, storage, and loss reduction).
  • World Vegetable Center (AVRDC) (free variety trials, IPM, and training materials for African producers).
  • International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA) (free agronomy and post-harvest resources for African horticulture).
  • International Trade Centre (ITC) (free market briefs and export standards for onion and shallot trade).

Prepared for Rise AFRICA Skills â Onion Farming, Module: Introduction to Onion Farming. All figures are indicative and should be verified against current national statistics before investment decisions.

quiz.q: Which continent produced over 20 million tonnes of onions in 2022?
quiz.explanation: Africa produced over 20 million tonnes of onions in 2022, with Egypt, Nigeria, and South Africa leading.

quiz.explanation: Bulb onions typically take 90-120 days from transplanting to harvest.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a common variety of bulb onion in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Red Creole is a popular short-day bulb onion variety grown in Africa.

quiz.q: What is a key characteristic of bunching onions?
options: B) They are harvested young for green leaves
C) They are only grown in Europe
D) They require 6 months to mature
quiz.explanation: Bunching onions are harvested young for their green leaves and mild flavor.

quiz.q: Which type of onion is prized in West African cuisine and grows in clusters?
quiz.explanation: Shallots are small, mild-flavored bulbs that grow in clusters and are prized in West African cuisine.

quiz.q: What is a major challenge in the onion industry in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Post-harvest losses can reach 30-50% due to poor storage, which is a major challenge.

quiz.q: Which country is the largest onion producer in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Egypt leads Africa with about 3.5 million tonnes of onions produced in 2022.

quiz.q: What is the global onion production figure for 2022?
quiz.explanation: Global onion production reached about 100 million tonnes in 2022.

quiz.q: Why do onion prices fluctuate seasonally?
options: B) Due to supply and demand
quiz.explanation: Prices fluctuate because during the dry season, supply is low, so prices can double.

quiz.q: What is a key trend in the onion market?
options: A) Decreased demand for red onions
B) Growth in processed onion products
quiz.explanation: There is growth in processed onion products like powder and paste, which adds value.

quiz.q: How many calories are in 100g of onion?
quiz.explanation: A 100g serving of onion provides about 40 calories.

quiz.q: Which nutrient is NOT commonly found in onions?
quiz.explanation: Onions are rich in vitamin C, potassium, and quercetin, but not vitamin B12.

quiz.q: What is the potential income for a smallholder farmer with 1 hectare of onions?
quiz.explanation: A smallholder farmer with 1 hectare can earn between $2,000 and $5,000 per season.

quiz.q: Which value-added product can be made from onions?
quiz.explanation: Onions can be processed into powder, paste, pickles, juice, and oil, among other products.

quiz.q: What is the life cycle of an onion plant?
quiz.explanation: Onions are biennial, completing their life cycle in two years.

quiz.q: How deep do onion roots typically grow?
quiz.explanation: Onion roots are shallow, mostly in the top 30cm of soil.

quiz.q: What triggers bulb formation in onions?
quiz.explanation: Bulb formation is triggered when days get longer, typically more than 12 hours of daylight.

quiz.q: Which variety is best for equatorial regions in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Short-day varieties like Red Creole are best for equatorial regions.

quiz.q: What causes the pungent smell of onions?
quiz.explanation: Sulfur compounds released when cells are damaged cause the pungent smell and tears.

quiz.q: What is a recommended spacing for onion plants?
quiz.explanation: Proper spacing of 10-15cm between plants ensures good air circulation.

quiz.q: Which career involves raising seedlings for farmers?
quiz.explanation: Nursery operators raise seedlings for farmers who prefer transplants.

quiz.q: How much can a kilogram of certified onion seed sell for?
quiz.explanation: A kilogram of certified onion seed can sell for $50-$100.

quiz.q: What is a role of an agricultural extension officer?
options: B) Advising farmers on best practices
quiz.explanation: Agricultural extension officers advise farmers on best practices.

quiz.q: What margin can a trader make when buying and selling onions?
quiz.explanation: A trader can make a 20-30% margin by buying from farmers and selling to urban markets.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of joining a cooperative?
quiz.explanation: Cooperatives help farmers access better markets and negotiate prices.

quiz.q: Which of these is a storage method for onions?
quiz.explanation: Ventilated stores are commonly used to store onions and reduce post-harvest losses.

quiz.q: What is the first step to start an onion farming business?
quiz.explanation: Starting small and learning is the recommended first step before scaling up.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a pest that attacks onion leaves?
quiz.explanation: Thrips, aphids, and whiteflies are common pests that attack onion leaves.

quiz.q: What is a disease that affects onions?
quiz.explanation: Purple blotch is a common fungal disease that affects onion leaves.

options: C) Used only for local consumption
quiz.explanation: Onion farming in Nigeria employs over 1 million people across the value chain.
